To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
genetically engineered enzymes used in flavour and fragrance production are potent allergens and can cause occupational asthma.
the use of genetically engineered (GE) enzymes in the synthesis and processing of food and other products is increasing tremendously.
sensitisation to genetically modified enzymes is a major occupational health problem, which is not sufficiently recognised by regulatory authorities and employers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the sensitising potential of genetically modified enzymes in occupational settings.
the development of suitable diagnostic tools to monitor sensitisation to genetically modified enzymes in exposed subjects.
the development and validation of new methods for specific IgE detection of genetically modified enzymes in occupational settings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of genetically engineered products in occupational settings should be accompanied by regular surveillance including biomarker testing.
the use of genetically engineered enzyme preparations in the synthesis of flavours, fragrances and detergents is not without risk.
the sensitisation and allergy to enzymes in general, including those derived from recombinant DNA technology, should be considered as a major occupational health hazard.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

genetically modified enzymes used to produce flavourings and fragrances can elicit sensitisation and allergic symptoms, and the lack of commercial diagnostic tools for the detection of specific IgE against modified enzymes is a major problem.
the genetically modified enzymes are allergens and that they should be considered in the diagnosis of occupational asthma and other work-related respiratory diseases.
genetically engineered enzymes used as flavour enhancers, fragrances and detergents are potent sensitising agents and that the sensitisation risk is higher than previously assumed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of genetically engineered proteins in the production of flavourings, detergents, food additives, pharmaceuticals, etc, should be accompanied by a mandatory allergenicity test.
the sensitisation and allergy to enzymes used in occupational settings can be detected by the specific fluorescence assay and that the results correlate with work-related symptoms.
the sensitisation risk is underestimated and that the use of genetically engineered proteins as food additives and flavourings needs to be reconsidered.
